newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Wienerberger sell-off gets market applause. [CORRECTED 12:27 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Wienerberger sell-off gets market applause. [CORRECTED 12:27 GMT]

text.p: Wienerberger, the world's biggest brick maker, said on Monday it would spin off its Treibacher abrasive materials unit to a German group to cement its top position in the European building materials industry.
Share analysts applauded the move and Wienerberger shares rose.

Wienerberger Baustoffindustrie said it had sold majority control of artificial corundum maker Treibacher Schleifmittel to Germany's August von Finck family group for an undisclosed sum. Treibacher's management would take on 10 percent of the shares, it added.
Sister unit Treibacher Industrie, which makes alloys for the steel industry, will remain part of the Wienerberger group.

Wienerberger, which is majority controlled by Austria's Creditanstalt and Belgium's Koramic now operates more than 150 plants on three continents. Koramic shares gained 40 Belgian francs to 2,195 in Brussels.
(Corrects by removing reference to booking a gain).

"We want to continue our ascent in the international building materials industry," Wienerberger spokesman Gerhard Bachmaier told Reuters. "We want to use the proceeds to make further aquisitions in the building materials area."

Treibacher Schleifmittel, which employs 930 and has plants in Austria, Germany, Italy, Slovenia and North America, reported 1996 pre-tax profits of 10 million schillings on sales of 1.5 billion schillings. Wienerberger's 1996 group sales were at 15.06 billion schillings.

"The reason for the sale is the implementation of the company's strategy. It envisions an even stronger concentration on the core building materials business and stepping up expansion in new foreign markets," Wienerberger said.
Analysts nodded their approval and investors greeted the deal by pushing up Wienerberger's shares 18.85 schillings to 2,539.85 in midday trading in Vienna.
"I think this is very good for Wienerberger. They're divesting a non-core business with very low margins," said Robin Horne, Austria analyst at Kleinwort Benson in London.
The deal came just three weeks after Wienerberger sold a key Vienna office and retail complex to a local real estate fund for three billion schillings in cash and liabilities.

The group over the past few years has made a string of acquisitions to expand its hold on the world's brick market, including Belgium's Terca Bricks in April of last year and France' Sturm in the second half of 1995.

Industry insiders had long expected the group to spin off one or both of its Treibacher units after Wienerberger chief executive Gerhard Schaschl told a news conference last month: "We love Treibacher, but nothing lasts forever."
Kleinwort's Horne noted the company had cleverly split Treibacher Schleifmittel, which is burdened by losses in its North American operations, from highly profitable Treibacher Industrie.
But he added Wienerberger's reorganisation drive may well continue with the sale of Treibacher Industrie. "It wouldn't surprise me if they sell the Industrie unit as well," he said.

Wienerberger said the sale of Treibacher Schleifmittel would put a damper on 1997 group sales while having little, if any, impact on current-year earnings. "We expect sales of about 15 billion schillings this year and our pre-tax prognosis remains at two billion schillings," the spokesman said.
